**Wikipedia: A Short Overview**

Wikipedia is a free, multilingual, web-based encyclopedia that anyone can edit. It was launched on January 15, 2001, by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger, and is operated by the Wikimedia Foundation, a U.S.-based nonprofit [1][2]. It runs on the open-source MediaWiki platform, and its content is released under free licenses (Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike), allowing reuse and adaptation with attribution [1][2]. As of 2025, it exists in over 300 language editions with more than 60 million articles total, nearly 7 million of them in English [1][3].

Wikipedia is funded by donations rather than advertising, and its content is written entirely by volunteers — roughly 250,000+ active editors per month across all editions [2][3]. Content decisions are made by community consensus rather than by the Foundation, guided by the "Five Pillars" [1][4]. Three core content policies govern articles: **neutral point of view** (representing significant published views fairly and proportionately, with "due weight"), **verifiability** (claims must be attributable to published reliable sources — "verifiability, not truth"), and **no original research** (no unpublished analysis, novel interpretations, or synthesis of sources) [1][2][3][4]. Transparency and quality-control tools include full page revision histories, talk pages, watchlists, vandalism-reverting bots, and escalating dispute-resolution mechanisms up to the volunteer Arbitration Committee [4].

Reliability has been debated since its founding. A landmark 2005 *Nature* study found English Wikipedia's science articles roughly comparable in accuracy to Encyclopædia Britannica, though quality varies by topic and article maturity [5]. Documented problems include vandalism and hoaxes (e.g., the Seigenthaler false biography of 2005), factual errors in medical articles, systemic demographic bias among editors (predominantly male, Global North–based) leading to content gaps, disputed ideological bias, undisclosed paid editing, state-influence concerns, and citation rot [7][9][10][11][12][14][16][17][18].

**References**

[1] Wikipedia, "Wikipedia" / "About Wikipedia"
[2] Wikimedia Foundation, "Our Projects" / FAQ
[3] Wikimedia Statistics; Wikipedia "List of Wikipedias"
[4] Wikipedia: "Five Pillars," "Verifiability," "No Original Research," "Administrators"
[5] Giles, J., "Internet encyclopaedias go head to head," *Nature* 438 (2005)
[7] Seigenthaler, J., "A False Wikipedia 'Biography,'" *USA Today* (2005)
[9] Hasty et al., *PLOS ONE* (2014)
[10] WMF Community Insights / editor surveys; Wikipedia: Systemic bias
[11] Greenstein & Zhu, *Management Science* (2018)
[12] Rozado, D., Manhattan Institute (2024)
[14] U.S. House Oversight Committee letter to Wikimedia Foundation (2025)
[16] WMF sockpuppet bans re: Wiki-PR (2013)
[17] WMF ban of seven editors over Chinese-language infiltration (2021)
[18] Douglass et al., "Citation Needed" (2016)
